title: Texture-Based Breast Cancer Nodule Classification in Ultrasound Imaging Using Adaptive Median Filtering and MLP
abstract: The Ultrasonography (USG) is an imaging technique used to identify breast abnormalities. The benefits of ultrasound imaging encompass its non-invasive nature and absence of radiation exposure. Nonetheless, ultrasound imaging outcomes often involve issues that cause variations in physicians' interpretations of breast ultrasound images. Computer-Aided Diagnosis (CAD) is a computational approach that offers an objective secondary assessment in identifying the attributes of nodules in breast ultrasound images. The CAD method includes an image preparation phase that encompasses RoI selection, filtering, texture feature extraction, and classification. The filtering procedure is executed utilizing a median adaptive filter and a median filter. Texture feature extraction is performed with nine histogram features and 21 Gray Level Co-occurrence Matrix (GLCM) features. Extraction results from Scilab indicate that employing 30 texture features enables the Multi Layer Perceptron (MLP) to categorize cystic and solid mass nodules with an accuracy of 88.89%, while utilizing 10 texture features yields an accuracy of 80.56%.

title: Quantum and Supercomputer Technology and Their Comparative Analysis
abstract: This article comprehensively examines the conceptual and practical aspects of two fundamental directions at the peak of the hierarchy of modern computing technologies — classical supercomputers and quantum computing systems. The relevance of the research is explained by the rapid growth of data volumes and the fact that traditional silicon technologies have reached their physical limits. The first part of the article analyzes the history of supercomputer development, their multi-core parallel architecture, and operating principles based on logical bits. Simultaneously, the technological limitations of such systems, including high energy consumption and cooling requirements, are highlighted. The second part explores the laws of quantum mechanics as the theoretical foundation of quantum computers, specifically the impact of superposition and entanglement phenomena on computing efficiency. The fundamental differences between classical bits and quantum bits (qubits) are scientifically justified, alongside the revolutionary potential of quantum algorithms (such as Shor’s and Grover’s algorithms) in traditional cryptographic and search systems. In the final section, a comparative analysis of these two powerful systems is conducted regarding processing speed, energy consumption, fault tolerance, and practical application areas. The research results indicate that quantum computers will not entirely replace classical supercomputers in the near future; instead, they will facilitate the formation of hybrid computing models. The article is intended for industry specialists, students, and those interested in the evolution of high technologies.

title: The Causal Poset Transformer with Reflective Memory: Sparse Write Self Token Memory (SWSTM) as a New Associative Primitive
abstract: We present the Sparse Write Self‑Token Memory (SWSTM), the minimal differentiable content‑addressable memory that proves exact associative recall (MSE = 0.000000) on random key‑value pairs and achieves 89.8% accuracy on a 64‑pair sequential RAM task, while a standard Transformer collapses to 11.5%. Ablation studies confirm that three components are jointly necessary: competitive sparse top‑1 write, a learned prototype address space, and a temporal self‑token. This paper merges the minimal synthetic proof (exact recall, birthday‑paradox collision analysis, self‑token collision‑resolution demo) with the full sequential RAM task at scale, providing the rigorous experimental foundation for all subsequent scaling work. Code is released under MIT license.

title: Engineering Protocol for Non-Local Quantum State Translation via Triangular Synchronization and Lyapunov-Stabilized Voronkov Loops.
abstract: This technical protocol defines a deterministic method for non-local quantum state translation. The system utilizes active Lyapunov-based stabilization within "Voronkov Loops" to prevent decoherence. State transfer is achieved via a Triangular Synchronization mechanism (TS-Protocol) and global attractor switching, enabling high-fidelity translation of quantum information between nodes while maintaining topological protection.

title: RISE OF SHADOWS: DEVELOPMENT OF A 2D ANDROID DUNGEON CRAWLER WITH AI DRIVEN GAMEPLAY MECHANICS AND PROCEDURAL GENERATION
authors: Priya Bhagat and Assi Prof. Dr. Meena Mashru
abstract: This paper presents the design, architecture, and implementation of Rise of Shadows, a native 2D actionadventure dungeon crawler developed for the Android platform. The game addresses prevalent shortcomings in existing mobile dungeon crawlers — namely repetitive level design, rudimentary enemy behaviour, and imprecise touch controls — by integrating procedural dungeon generation, A* pathfinding-based enemy AI, dual-stick virtual joystick controls, and performance-focused rendering using Android's SurfaceView API. The system is implemented in Java using Android Studio and employs a modular, scalable architecture comprising discrete subsystems for player control, enemy logic, bullet physics, collision detection, sound management, and game state transitions. Object pooling is used to minimise garbage collection overhead, ensuring smooth frame rates on mid-range Android devices. Testing encompassed functional unit tests, integration tests across modules, and non-functional performance and compatibility assessments. Results confirm stable gameplay with dynamic difficulty scaling across five progressive levels. The paper further discusses the game's architectural decisions, algorithmic underpinnings, and future enhancement pathways including multiplayer support, leaderboard integration, and procedural narrative elements.

title: Fine-Tuning Pre-Trained Code Models for AI-Generated Code Detection
abstract: This paper describes the system submitted by team \textbf{Archaeology} to SemEval-2026 Task~13 on AI-generated code detection. The shared task consists of three subtasks; we participate in Subtask-A (binary classification: human-written vs.\ AI-generated code) and Subtask-B (11-class attribution of the generating model). Starting from a TF-IDF and Logistic Regression baseline, we fine-tune four pre-trained code models (CodeBERT, GraphCodeBERT, UniXcoder, and CodeT5+) with separate strategies for each subtask. For Subtask-A, we use leave-one-language-out cross-validation, code augmentation, chunked inference with trimmed-mean aggregation, and threshold calibration on a difficult dataset. For Subtask-B, we use sandwich token packing, class-balanced loss, and multi-seed ensembling with test-time augmentation. Our best submissions obtain macro-F1 scores of 0.737 on Subtask-A (6th/81 teams) and 0.422 on Subtask-B (7th/34 teams).

title: Feature Selection Optimization Using Hybrid Genetic Algorithm and Recursive Feature Elimination for High-Dimensional Data.
abstract: High-dimensional datasets, commonly encountered in domains such as bioinformatics, text mining, and financial analytics, often suffer from the curse of dimensionality, leading to increased computational complexity and reduced model performance. Effective feature selection is therefore essential to enhance classification accuracy while minimizing redundancy and irrelevant information. This study proposes a hybrid feature selection framework that integrates a Genetic Algorithm (GA) with Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE) to address the limitations of traditional methods. The Genetic Algorithm is employed as a global search strategy to explore the feature space and identify promising subsets, while RFE is utilized as a local optimization technique to iteratively eliminate less significant features based on model-specific importance scores. The proposed GA–RFE hybrid approach aims to balance exploration and exploitation, enabling efficient identification of optimal feature subsets in high-dimensional environments. The framework is evaluated on multiple benchmark datasets characterized by large feature spaces. Performance is assessed using standard evaluation metrics, including classification accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score, alongside computational efficiency. Experimental results demonstrate that the hybrid method significantly outperforms standalone GA, RFE, and traditional dimensionality reduction techniques such as Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and LASSO in terms of both predictive performance and feature reduction. Furthermore, the proposed approach achieves a substantial reduction in feature dimensionality without compromising model robustness, thereby facilitating faster training and improved generalization. The findings highlight the effectiveness of combining evolutionary optimization with recursive elimination for feature selection in complex datasets. This research contributes to the development of scalable and intelligent feature selection techniques and provides a practical solution for handling high-dimensional data in real-world machine learning applications.
